title: Give & receive I: あげる・くれる・もらう (things)

grammarPoints.rule: Japanese has no single verb for give. Which one you reach for depends on WHICH WAY the thing moved past you — not on who is talking, and not on politeness. There is a circle drawn around you and the people who belong to you (うち, inside); everybody else stands そと, outside.

rows.subject: left
rows.note: The thing leaves the circle. I am what the sentence is about.

rows.subject: right
rows.note: Same present, arrow reversed. My friend is the subject — and I drop out, because くれる can only point at me.

examples.ja: ともだちに プレゼントを あげる。
examples.en: I'll give my friend a present.

examples.ja: ともだちが プレゼントを くれる。
examples.en: My friend gives me a present.

examples.ja: ははは せんせいに はなを あげる。
examples.en: My mother gives the teacher flowers.

examples.ja: ちちが おおきい とけいを くれる。
examples.en: My father gives me a big watch.

examples.ja: あには がくせいに じしょを あげる。
examples.en: My older brother gives the student a dictionary.

antiPattern.ja: ともだちが プレゼントを あげる。
antiPattern.why: あげる's arrow leaves your side and can never land back on it, so this sentence never arrives anywhere — a thing coming in from outside takes くれる: ともだちが プレゼントを くれる。

grammarPoints.rule: Every に you have met since module 5 has been a place — 「がっこうに いく。」 に marks where something ENDS UP, and a transfer is a journey with a person at the far end. That is why the recipient takes に whether the far end is a station or a sister. Now put it on a pair where the thing comes BACK: かす is to lend, かりる is to borrow, one loan seen from its two ends.

rows.subject: left
rows.note: I lend. The umbrella leaves my side — and comes back later.

rows.subject: left
rows.note: I borrow. Arrow reversed, but に stays put on my friend — the same particle, the far end of the same journey.

examples.ja: ともだちに かさを かりる。
examples.en: I borrow an umbrella from my friend.

examples.ja: いもうとに おかねを かす。
examples.en: I lend my little sister money.

examples.ja: あねは せんせいに てがみを あげる。
examples.en: My older sister gives the teacher a letter.

examples.ja: だれに おみやげを あげる？
examples.en: Who are you giving the souvenir to?

examples.ja: おとうとに じてんしゃを かした。
examples.en: I lent my little brother my bicycle.

antiPattern.ja: ともだちに かさを かす。
antiPattern.why: かす hands the umbrella over and かりる takes one in — if the umbrella is coming to you, the verb is かりる: ともだちに かさを かりる。

grammarPoints.rule: Third verb, and it rearranges the sentence rather than just pointing it. The subject of もらう is whoever ENDS UP HOLDING THE THING. Then the part that catches everybody: the person it came FROM also takes に. One rule, not two — に marks the OTHER PERSON in the transfer, and the verb decides which end they are standing at. English does the same trick: you give TO somebody, you hear it FROM somebody.

rows.subject: right
rows.note: About the teacher, and what the teacher did.

rows.subject: left
rows.note: SAME arrow, same event. Only the subject moved — now the sentence is about me and what I ended up with, and に marks where it came from.

examples.ja: せんせいに じしょを もらう。
examples.en: I get a dictionary from the teacher.

examples.ja: いしゃに くすりを もらう。
examples.en: I get medicine from the doctor.

examples.ja: いしゃに くすりを もらう。

examples.ja: かいしゃの ひとに おかしを もらう。
examples.en: I get sweets from the people at the company.

antiPattern.ja: せんせいは じしょを もらう。
antiPattern.why: the subject of もらう is whoever ends up holding the thing, so this says the TEACHER is the one who got a dictionary — if you are the one who received it, you are the subject: せんせいに じしょを もらう。

grammarPoints.rule: The source of a もらう can be marked に or から, and both are correct: 「ともだちに おみやげを もらう。」 「ともだちから おみやげを もらう。」 Nobody will correct either. から is module 4's word and has always meant the starting point — 「にほんから きた」 — so all that has changed is that a person is now allowed to be one. に is the tighter, more ordinary choice and what you hear most in speech; から is more explicit about the source, and it is what people reach for when the giver is an organisation. There is one case where から is the answer rather than a preference: when the source is not a person at all. 「かいしゃから きねんの とけいを もらう。」 A company is a place as much as a giver, and に there starts to read as a destination. あげる and くれる have no source slot, so から never appears with them — a から is a quiet signal that もらう is coming.

antiPattern.ja: ともだちから プレゼントを あげる。
antiPattern.why: から marks where a thing came from and あげる has no source slot — only もらう can take a から: ともだちから プレゼントを もらう。

grammarPoints.rule: Here is the one hard ban in this module. あげる CANNOT POINT AT YOU. 「わたしに プレゼントを あげる」 is not awkward or impolite — it is broken, the way I gave me a present is broken in English, and a Japanese speaker will not work out what you meant. あげる's arrow leaves your circle, so there is nowhere for it to land if the destination is inside the circle it just left. The moment a thing is arriving at you, あげる is off the table and you pick between two verbs — and the choice is about what the sentence is ABOUT, not about the event. くれる if the giver is the news: 「ともだちが プレゼントを くれる。」 もらう if what you ended up with is the news: 「ともだちに プレゼントを もらう。」 The circle stretches too, and your family is inside it. 「ともだちが いもうとに おかしを くれる」 is fine — the sweets came in to my side even though they did not come to my hand. Say あげる there and you have pushed your own sister outside the circle.

examples.ja: ともだちが わたしに プレゼントを くれる。
examples.en: My friend gives me a present.

examples.ja: ともだちに プレゼントを もらう。
examples.en: I get a present from my friend.

examples.ja: せんせいが いもうとに おかしを くれる。
examples.en: The teacher gives my little sister sweets.

examples.ja: がくせいに ノートを あげる。
examples.en: I'll give the student a notebook.

examples.ja: ともだちが ケーキを くれるから うれしい。
examples.en: My friend is giving me a cake, so I'm happy.

antiPattern.ja: ともだちが わたしに プレゼントを あげる。
antiPattern.why: あげる's arrow leaves your side and can never land back on you — a thing arriving at you takes くれる: ともだちが わたしに プレゼントを くれる。

grammarPoints.rule: Put the three verbs in the past and the module becomes usable, because most of what anybody says about a gift is said afterwards. The forms are module 11's. あげる and くれる are る-verbs: drop る, add た — あげた, くれた. もらう is an う-verb ending in う, so it takes かう's った row: もらった. Nothing new to memorise. What IS worth watching is that the direction does not soften in the past. 「ともだちが けいたいを くれた」 still points in at me; 「ともだちに けいたいを あげた」 still points out. English collapses both back to gave, so say the arrow to yourself before you pick the verb. 「もらった」 is the most useful of the three, because it answers the question the past tense invites: 「その とけい、いいね。」 「たんじょうびに ちちに もらった。」 Nice watch — I got it from my father for my birthday.

examples.ja: たんじょうびに ちちに とけいを もらった。
examples.en: I got a watch from my father for my birthday.

examples.ja: ともだちが けいたいを くれた。
examples.en: My friend gave me a mobile phone.

examples.ja: せんせいに はなたばを あげた。
examples.en: I gave the teacher a bouquet.

examples.ja: プレゼントを もらったから うれしかった。
examples.en: I got a present, so I was happy.

examples.ja: いしゃに くすりを もらったから あした がっこうに いく。
examples.en: I got medicine from the doctor, so I'll go to school tomorrow.

antiPattern.ja: たんじょうびに ちちに とけいを あげった。
antiPattern.why: あげる is a る-verb, so its past is あげた — った belongs to う-verbs like もらう: たんじょうびに ちちに とけいを もらった。

grammarPoints.rule: Two more words, and for now you only have to RECOGNISE them. When the giver is somebody you look up to — a teacher, a customer, somebody much older — Japanese swaps the verb rather than adding a polite ending. くれる becomes くださる, もらう becomes いただく. 「せんせいが じしょを くださった。」 The teacher was kind enough to give me a dictionary. 「せんせいに じしょを いただいた。」 I received a dictionary from the teacher. Notice the axis has not moved an inch: くださる points in at me exactly like くれる, and いただく makes the receiver the subject exactly like もらう. Respect is a layer sitting on top of direction, which is why direction comes first. Meet them now because you will hear them constantly and cannot derive them — no rule you own gets you from くれる to くださった. When you are the one speaking, keep using くれる and もらう. Nobody will think you rude.

examples.en: The teacher was kind enough to give me a dictionary.

examples.ja: せんせいに じしょを いただいた。

examples.ja: たなかさんが おいわいの はなたばを くださる。
examples.en: Tanaka is kind enough to give me a congratulatory bouquet.

antiPattern.ja: ともだちが おかしを くださった。
antiPattern.why: くださる is for somebody you look up to, so using it of a friend puts a stranger between you — a friend takes くれる: ともだちが おかしを くれた。

grammarPoints.rule: You have had 〜たい since module 13 and it works on these three verbs unchanged: drop る or う, add たい. あげたい. もらいたい. What is worth a lesson is that wanting cuts across the direction axis rather than sitting on it. 「せんせいに はなたばを あげたい。」 I want to give the teacher a bouquet — the arrow still points out, and たい only says I have not done it yet. 「たんじょうびに ケーキを もらいたい。」 I want to get a cake for my birthday — still the receiver's side, still もらう's shape. There is one gap worth knowing about now rather than being surprised by later: 〜たい is for YOUR OWN wanting. You cannot use it to say what somebody else wants, which is why every example here is about you. And くれる has no たい at all, because it would mean wanting somebody else to do something — a different form entirely, and not this module's.

examples.ja: せんせいに はなたばを あげたい。
examples.en: I want to give the teacher a bouquet.

examples.ja: たんじょうびに ケーキを もらいたい。
examples.en: I want to get a cake for my birthday.

examples.ja: がくせいに ノートを あげたい。
examples.en: I want to give the student a notebook.

examples.ja: はなが すきだから はなたばを もらいたい。

examples.ja: ともだちに おれいの カードを あげたい。

antiPattern.ja: せんせいに はなたばを あげる たい。
antiPattern.why: 〜たい attaches to the verb stem, not to the finished dictionary form — あげる loses its る before たい: せんせいに はなたばを あげたい。

grammarPoints.rule: Because くれる and もらう already say which way the thing moved, Japanese stops mentioning you. 「ともだちが けいたいを くれた。」 There is no わたしに in that sentence and there does not need to be — くれる cannot point anywhere else. Same with もらう: 「ちちに おかねを もらった」 has no わたしは, because the subject of もらう is the speaker unless somebody else is named. This is not an abbreviation of a longer sentence; it is the payoff for having direction built into the verb. And it works the other way round. If you DO say わたしは, you are contrasting: 「わたしは かさを もらった」 lands as I got an umbrella, whatever everyone else got — module 3's は marking a topic against a background. So when you hear くれる with no receiver, the receiver is the speaker or somebody on their side; when you hear もらう with no subject, the subject is the speaker.

examples.en: My friend gave me a mobile phone.

examples.ja: ちちに おかねを もらった。
examples.en: I got money from my father.

examples.ja: わたしは かさを もらった。
examples.en: I got an umbrella.

antiPattern.why: くれる is what carries a thing to your side, and it carries it without needing わたしに at all: ともだちが けいたいを くれた。

beats.stem: びょうきの ときに ともだちが くだものを
beats.answer: くれた
beats.en: When I was ill my friend gave me some fruit
beats.explanation: the fruit came to me while I was ill, so くれる is the verb and it has already happened. あげた would send it to my friend, and かりた would mean I have to give it back.
